paper_design_summary: The authors classify 41,298,433 OpenAlex papers in six natural-science disciplines (1980-2025) as AI-augmented or not with a fine-tuned BERT model (F1 0.875 against expert labels) and compare AI and non-AI papers and their authors. Diversity of science's focus is measured as the 'knowledge extent' (maximum distance to the centroid) of 1,000-paper samples in SPECTER 2.0 embedding space, plus knowledge entropy and follow-on citation engagement. AI covers machine learning, deep learning, and generative AI eras; a 2023-2025 subset is replicated in the supplement.

eligibility.reason: Observational comparison of AI-augmented and non-AI papers in a corpus of 41,298,433 OpenAlex natural-science papers; no people are randomly assigned to generative-AI assistance (pp. 1-2; pp. 8-9, Methods M1-M3). Diversity is scored on published paper outputs using knowledge extent and entropy (p. 5, Fig. 3c-d; pp. 6 and 11, Methods M8). The diversity analyses count paper samples and citation families, with no analyzed participant count reported for these comparisons, so the at-least-50-people criterion is unclear (p. 11, Methods M8-M9); counts from the separate career analyses are not participant counts for these diversity comparisons. 'AI' includes conventional machine-learning and deep-learning methods as well as generative AI (p. 2; p. 24, Supplementary Note 1.3). The 4,797,614-paper subset is defined by publication during the generative-AI era, 2023-2025, not by verified use of generative AI; its AI-augmented category still includes any detected AI method (p. 8, Methods M2; p. 28, Supplementary Note 4.1; pp. 57-59, Supplementary Figs S28-S30). In the ranking pooled across all selected disciplines, CNN and SVM rank first and second in 2023, 2024 and 2025, while LLM ranks sixth, fourth and third, respectively (p. 70, Supplementary Table S5). No reported diversity comparison isolates generative-AI users. Core remains no; retained as observational context on broader AI use, with its relevance to the generative-AI section requiring the Review 1 scope decision.

one_line_finding: Across 41.3 million natural-science papers (1980-2025), AI-method use is associated with a 4.63% smaller median collective knowledge extent across science, with a contraction in each of the six disciplines (χ² ≥ 84.05, p < 0.001 in each; arXiv v4 p. 6, Results 'AI contracts science's focus'; p. 5, Fig. 3c), and 22.00% less follow-on engagement (p. 6); the 2023-2025 replication shows a consistent knowledge-extent pattern but is selected by publication date and does not isolate generative-AI use (p. 28, Supplementary Note 4.1; p. 58, Fig. S29; p. 70, Table S5).

applied.old: Across 41.3 million natural-science papers (1980-2025), papers that use AI methods, mostly pre-generative machine learning, cover a 4.63% smaller median knowledge extent in SPECTER 2.0 embedding space than non-AI papers in all six disciplines (χ2 ≥ 84.05, p < 0.001; arXiv v4 p. 6, Fig. 3c), and their follow-on papers engage with each other 22.00% less (p. 6); the generative-AI-era subset is described as consistent but shown only in Supplementary Fig. S29 (p. 58).

applied.old: Observational comparison of AI-augmented and non-AI papers in a corpus of 41,298,433 OpenAlex natural-science papers; no one is assigned to AI. The diversity outcome is the knowledge extent of paper embeddings (p. 6, Fig. 3c). Scope caveat: 'AI' means any AI method detected in a paper's title and abstract across machine-learning (1980-2014), deep-learning (2015-2022), and generative-AI (2023-) eras, mostly research tools such as SVMs and CNNs rather than generative AI used for writing or ideation (pp. 2, 8). Only the 2023-2025 subset of 4,797,614 papers bears on generative AI, and it is reported as figures only (Supplementary Figs S28-S30, pp. 57-59). Review 1 may judge the paper out of scope.
